Learning Optimal Representations with the Decodable Information Bottleneck

Yann Dubois
Facebook AI Research
yannd@fb.com
&Douwe Kiela
Facebook AI Research
dkiela@fb.com
&David J. Schwab
Facebook AI Research
CUNY Graduate Center
dschwab@fb.com
&Ramakrishna Vedantam
Facebook AI Research
ramav@fb.com
Abstract

We address the question of characterizing and finding optimal representations for supervised learning. Traditionally, this question has been tackled using the Information Bottleneck, which compresses the inputs while retaining information about the targets, in a decoder-agnostic fashion. In machine learning, however, our goal is not compression but rather generalization, which is intimately linked to the predictive family or decoder of interest (e.g. linear classifier). We propose the Decodable Information Bottleneck (DIB) that considers information retention and compression from the perspective of the desired predictive family. As a result, DIB gives rise to representations that are optimal in terms of expected test performance and can be estimated with guarantees. Empirically, we show that the framework can be used to enforce a small generalization gap on downstream classifiers and to predict the generalization ability of neural networks.

1 Introduction

linecolor=red,backgroundcolor=red!25,bordercolor=red,]YD: Review all appendices so that there are references in order A fundamental choice in supervised machine learning (ML) centers around the data representation from which to perform predictions. While classical ML uses predefined encodings of the data [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] recent progress [6, 7] has been driven by learning such representations. A natural question, then, is what characterizes an “optimal” representation — in terms of generalization — and how to learn it.

The standard framework for studying generalization, statistical learning theory [8], usually assumes a fixed dataset/representation, and aims to restrict the predictive functional family 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V} (e.g. linear classifiers) such that empirical risk minimizers (ERMs) generalize.111Rather than defining learning in terms of deterministic hypotheses h∈ℋℎℋh\in\mathcal{H}, we consider the more general [9] case of probabilistic predictors 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}, in order to make a link with information theory. Here, we turn the problem on its head: we ask whether it is possible to enforce generalization by changing the representation of the inputs such that ERMs in 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V} perform well, irrespective of the complexity of 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}.

A common approach to representation learning consists of jointly training the classifier and representation by minimizing the empirical risk (which we call J-ERM). By only considering empirical risk, J-ERM is optimal in the infinite data limit (consistent; [10]), but the resulting representations do not favor classifiers that will generalize from finite samples. In contrast, the information bottleneck (IB) method [11] aims for representations that have minimal information about the inputs to avoid over-fitting, while having sufficient information about the labels [12]. While conceptually appealing and used in a range of applications [13, 14, 15, 16], IB is based on Shannon’s mutual information, which was developed for communication theory [17] and does not take into account the predictive family 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V} of interest. As a result, IB’s sufficiency requirement does not ensure the existence of a predictor f∈𝒱𝑓𝒱f\in\mathcal{V} that can perform well using the learned representation; 222As an illustration, IB invariance to bijections suggests that a non-linearly entangled representation is as good as a linearly separable one if there is a bijection between them, even when classifying using a logistic regression. while its minimality term is difficult to estimate, making IB impractical without resorting to approximations [18, 19, 20, 21].

We resolve these issues by introducing the decodable information bottleneck (DIB) objective, which recovers minimal sufficient representations relative to a predictive family 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}. Intuitively, it ensures that classifiers in 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V} can predict labels (𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-sufficiency) but cannot distinguish examples with the same label (𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality), as illustrated in fig. 1.

Our main contributions can be summarized as follows:

  • •

    We generalize notions of minimality and sufficiency to consider predictors 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V} of interest.

  • •

    We prove that such representations are optimal — every downstream ERM in 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V} reaches the best achievable test performance — and can be learned with guarantees using DIB.

  • •

    We experimentally demonstrate that using our representations can increase the performance and robustness of downstream classifiers in average and worst case scenarios.

  • •

    We show that the generalization ability of a neural network is highly correlated with the degree of 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality of its hidden representations in a wide range of settings (562 models).

Throughout this paper, we provide a more informal presentation in the main body, and refer the reader to the appendices for more precise statements. For details about our notation, see Appx. A.

2.2 Sufficiency, Minimality, and the Information Bottleneck (IB)

We review IB, an information theoretic method for supervised representation learning. IB is built upon the intuition that a representation ZZ\mathrm{Z} should be maximally informative about YY\mathrm{Y} (sufficient), but contain no additional information about XX\mathrm{X} (minimal) to avoid possible over-fitting. Specifically, the set of sufficient representations 𝒮𝒮\mathcal{S}{} and minimal sufficient ℳℳ\mathcal{M}{} representations are defined as:333As shown in Sec. C.1.1, this common [12, 24] definition is a generalization of minimal sufficient statistics [25] to stochastic statistics Z=T​(X,ϵ)Z𝑇Xitalic-ϵ\mathrm{Z}=T(\mathrm{X},\epsilon) where ϵitalic-ϵ\epsilon is a source of noise independent of XX\mathrm{X}.

𝒮:=arg⁡maxZ′⁡I⁡[Y;Z′]andℳ≔arg⁡minZ′∈𝒮⁡I⁡[X;Z′]formulae-sequenceassign𝒮subscriptsuperscriptZ′IYsuperscriptZ′and≔ℳsubscriptsuperscriptZ′𝒮IXsuperscriptZ′\mathcal{S}{}\vcentcolon=\arg\max_{\mathrm{Z}^{\prime}}\operatorname{I}\negthinspace\left[\mathrm{Y};\mathrm{Z}^{\prime}\right]\quad\text{and}\quad\mathcal{M}{}\coloneqq\arg\min_{\mathrm{Z}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}{}}\operatorname{I}\negthinspace\left[\mathrm{X};\mathrm{Z}^{\prime}\right] (1)

The IB criterion (to minimize) can then be interpreted [12] as the Lagrangian relaxation of Eq. 1:

ℒIB:=−I⁡[Y;Z]+β∗I⁡[X;Z]assignsubscriptℒIBIYZ𝛽IXZ\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{IB}}{}\vcentcolon=-\operatorname{I}\negthinspace\left[\mathrm{Y};\mathrm{Z}\right]+\beta*\operatorname{I}\negthinspace\left[\mathrm{X};\mathrm{Z}\right] (2)

Despite its intuitive appeal, IB suffers from the following theoretical and practical issues: 1 Lack of optimalityguarantees for Z∈ℳZℳ\mathrm{Z}\in\mathcal{M}{}. Generalization bounds based on I⁡[Z;X]IZX\operatorname{I}\negthinspace\left[\mathrm{Z};\mathrm{X}\right] are a step towards such guarantees [12, 26] but current bounds are still vacuous [27]. The strong performance of invertible neural networks [28, 29] also shows that a small I⁡[X;Z]IXZ\operatorname{I}\negthinspace\left[\mathrm{X};\mathrm{Z}\right] is not required for generalization; 2 ℒIBsubscriptℒIB\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{IB}}{}is hard to estimate with finite samples [30, 12]. One has to either restrict the considered setting [11, 31, 32], or optimize variational [18, 19, 20] or non-parametric [21] bounds; 3 ℒIBsubscriptℒIB\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{IB}}{}is invariant to bijections and thus does not favor simple decision boundaries [33] that can be achieved by a f∈𝒱𝑓𝒱f\in\mathcal{V}.

We stipulate that these known issues stem from a common cause: IB uses mutual information, which is agnostic to the predictive family 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V} of interest. To remedy this, we leverage the recently proposed 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-information [23] to formalize the notion of 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimal 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-sufficient representations.

3 Methods

In this section, we define 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimal 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-sufficient representations, prove that they are optimal in the two-player representation learning game, and discuss how to approximately learn them in practice.

3.1 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-Sufficiency and Best Achievable Performance

Let us study Alice’s best risk minf∈𝒱⁡R​(f,Z)subscript𝑓𝒱R𝑓Z\min_{f\in\mathcal{V}}\mathrm{R}(f,\mathrm{Z}) using a representation ZZ\mathrm{Z}. This tight lower bound on her performance looks strikingly similar to H𝒱⁡[Y|Z]subscriptH𝒱conditionalYZ\operatorname{H_{\mathcal{V}}}\negthinspace\left[\mathrm{Y}\,|\,\mathrm{Z}\right], which is controlled by I𝒱⁡[Z→Y]subscriptI𝒱→ZY\operatorname{I_{\mathcal{V}}}\negthinspace\left[\mathrm{Z}\rightarrow\mathrm{Y}\right] (see Eq. 5). As a result, if Bob maximizes I𝒱⁡[Z→Y]subscriptI𝒱→ZY\operatorname{I_{\mathcal{V}}}\negthinspace\left[\mathrm{Z}\rightarrow\mathrm{Y}\right], he will ensure that Alice can achieve the lowest loss.

A representation ZZ\mathrm{Z} is said to be 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-sufficient if it maximizes 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-information with the labels. We denote all such representations as 𝒮𝒱:=arg⁡maxZ′⁡I𝒱⁡[Z′→Y]assignsubscript𝒮𝒱subscriptsuperscriptZ′subscriptI𝒱→superscriptZ′Y\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{V}}{}\vcentcolon=\arg\max_{\mathrm{Z}^{\prime}}\operatorname{I_{\mathcal{V}}}\negthinspace\left[\mathrm{Z}^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathrm{Y}\right].

3.2 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality and Generalization

We have seen that 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-sufficiency ensures that Alice could achieve the best loss. In this section, we study what representations Bob should chose to guarantee that Alice’s ERMs will perform optimally by ensuring that any ERM generalizes beyond the training set.

ZZ\mathrm{Z} is 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimal 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-sufficient if it is 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-sufficient and has minimal average 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-information with y𝑦y decompositions of XX\mathrm{X}. Intuitively, a representation is 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimal if no predictor in 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V} can assign different predictions to examples with the same label. Consequently, predictors will not be able to distinguish train and test examples and must thus perfectly generalize. In this case, predictors will perform optimally as there is at least one which does (𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-sufficiency; Prop. 1). We formalize this intuition in Sec. C.3:

Theorem 1.

(Informal) Let 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V} be a predictive family, 𝒟​∼i.i.d.​PX,YM𝒟i.i.d.similar-tosuperscriptsubscript𝑃XY𝑀\mathcal{D}\overset{\raisebox{-2.0pt}{\smash{\text{\tiny i.i.d.}}}}{\sim}P_{\mathrm{X},\mathrm{Y}}^{M}{} a dataset, and assume labels YY\mathrm{Y} are a deterministic function of the inputs t​(X)𝑡Xt(\mathrm{X}). If Z∈ℳ𝒱Zsubscriptℳ𝒱\mathrm{Z}\in\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{V}}{} be 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimal 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-sufficient, then the expected test loss of any ERM f^∈𝒱^​(𝒟)^𝑓^𝒱𝒟\hat{f}{}\in\hat{\mathcal{V}}(\mathcal{D}) is the best achievable risk, i.e., R​(f^,Z)=minZ⁡minf∈𝒱⁡R​(f,Z)R^𝑓ZsubscriptZsubscript𝑓𝒱R𝑓Z\mathrm{R}(\hat{f}{},\mathrm{Z})=\min_{\mathrm{Z}}\min_{f\in\mathcal{V}}\mathrm{R}(f,\mathrm{Z}){}.

As all ERMs reach the best risk, so does their expectation, i.e., any Z∈ℳ𝒱Zsubscriptℳ𝒱\mathrm{Z}\in\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{V}}{} is optimal. We also show in Sec. C.4 that 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality and 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-sufficiency satisfy the following properties:

Proposition 2.

Let 𝒱⊆𝒱+𝒱superscript𝒱\mathcal{V}\subseteq\mathcal{V}^{+} be two families and 𝒰𝒰\mathcal{U}{} the universal one. If labels are deterministic:

  • •

    Recoverability The set of 𝒰𝒰\mathcal{U}{}-minimal 𝒰𝒰\mathcal{U}{}-sufficient representations corresponds to the minimal sufficient representations that t.v.i. in the domain of 𝒰𝒰\mathcal{U}{}, i.e., ℳ𝒰=ℳ∩𝒵subscriptℳ𝒰ℳ𝒵\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{U}}=\mathcal{M}\cap\mathcal{Z}.

  • •

    Monotonicity 𝒱+superscript𝒱\mathcal{V}^{+}-minimal 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-sufficient representations are 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimal 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-sufficient, i.e., arg⁡maxZ∈𝒮𝒱⁡I𝒱+⁡[Z→Dec​(X,𝒴)]⊆ℳ𝒱subscriptZsubscript𝒮𝒱subscriptIsuperscript𝒱→ZDecX𝒴subscriptℳ𝒱\arg\max_{\mathrm{Z}\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{V}}{}}\operatorname{I_{\mathcal{V}^{+}}}\negthinspace\left[\mathrm{Z}\rightarrow\mathrm{Dec}(\mathrm{X},\mathcal{Y}){}\right]\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{V}}{}.

  • •

    Characterization Z∈ℳ𝒱⇔Z∈𝒮𝒱iffZsubscriptℳ𝒱Zsubscript𝒮𝒱\mathrm{Z}\in\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{V}}{}\iff\mathrm{Z}\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{V}}{} and I𝒱⁡[Z→Dec​(X,𝒴)]=0subscriptI𝒱→ZDecX𝒴0\operatorname{I_{\mathcal{V}}}\negthinspace\left[\mathrm{Z}\rightarrow\mathrm{Dec}(\mathrm{X},\mathcal{Y}){}\right]{}=0.

The recoverability shows that our notion of 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimal 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-sufficiency is a generalization of minimal sufficiency. As a corollary, IB’s representations are optimal when Alice is unconstrained in her choice of predictors 𝒱=𝒰𝒱𝒰\mathcal{V}=\mathcal{U}{}. The monotonicity implies that minimality with respect to (w.r.t.) a larger 𝒱+superscript𝒱\mathcal{V}^{+} is also optimal. Finally, the characterizations property gives a simple way of testing for 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality.

3.3 Practical Optimization and Estimation

In the previous section we characterized optimal representations Z∗∈ℳ𝒱superscriptZsubscriptℳ𝒱\mathrm{Z}^{*}\in\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{V}}{}. Unfortunately, Bob cannot learn these Z∗superscriptZ\mathrm{Z}^{*} as it requires the underlying distribution PX,Ysubscript𝑃XYP_{\mathrm{X},\mathrm{Y}}. We will now show that he can nevertheless approximate Z∗superscriptZ\mathrm{Z}^{*} in a sample- and computationally- efficient manner.

Optimization. Learning Z∈ℳ𝒱Zsubscriptℳ𝒱\mathrm{Z}\in\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{V}}{} requires solving a constrained optimization problem. Similarly to IB, we minimize the decodable information bottleneck (DIB), a Lagrangian relaxation of Def. 2:

ℒDIB:=−I𝒱⁡[Z→Y]+β∗I𝒱⁡[Z→Dec​(X,𝒴)]assignsubscriptℒDIBsubscriptI𝒱→ZY𝛽subscriptI𝒱→ZDecX𝒴\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DIB}}{}\vcentcolon=-\operatorname{I_{\mathcal{V}}}\negthinspace\left[\mathrm{Z}\rightarrow\mathrm{Y}\right]+\beta*\operatorname{I_{\mathcal{V}}}\negthinspace\left[\mathrm{Z}\rightarrow\mathrm{Dec}(\mathrm{X},\mathcal{Y}){}\right]{} (8)

Notice that each I𝒱⁡[Z→⋅]subscriptI𝒱→Z⋅\operatorname{I_{\mathcal{V}}}\negthinspace\left[\mathrm{Z}\rightarrow\mathrm{\cdot}\right] has an internal optimization. In particular I𝒱⁡[Z→Dec​(X,𝒴)]subscriptI𝒱→ZDecX𝒴\operatorname{I_{\mathcal{V}}}\negthinspace\left[\mathrm{Z}\rightarrow\mathrm{Dec}(\mathrm{X},\mathcal{Y}){}\right]{} turns the problem into a min (over ZZ\mathrm{Z}) - max (over f∈𝒱𝑓𝒱f\in\mathcal{V}) optimization, which can be hard to optimize [38, 39]. We empirically compare methods for optimizing ℒDIBsubscriptℒDIB\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DIB}}{} in Sec. E.2 and show that joint gradient descent ascent performs well if we ensure that the norm of the learned representation cannot diverge.

Estimation. A major benefit of ℒDIBsubscriptℒDIB\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DIB}}{} over ℒIBsubscriptℒIB\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{IB}}{} is that it can be estimated with guarantees using finite samples. Namely, if Bob has access to a training set 𝒟​∼i.i.d.​PX,YM𝒟i.i.d.similar-tosuperscriptsubscript𝑃XY𝑀\mathcal{D}\overset{\raisebox{-2.0pt}{\smash{\text{\tiny i.i.d.}}}}{\sim}P_{\mathrm{X},\mathrm{Y}}^{M}{}, he can estimate ℒDIBsubscriptℒDIB\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DIB}}{} reasonably well. Despite these approximations, we show in Sec. C.5 that ℒDIBsubscriptℒDIB\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DIB}}{} inherits 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-information’s estimation bounds [23].

Proposition 3.

The fact that the estimation error in Prop. 3 grows with the (Rademacher) complexity of 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}, shows that the error is largest for 𝒱=𝒰𝒱𝒰\mathcal{V}=\mathcal{U}{} corresponding to ℒIBsubscriptℒIB\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{IB}}{}. We also see a trade-off in Alice’s choice of 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}. A more complex 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V} means the estimation of ℒ^DIB​(𝒟)subscript^ℒDIB𝒟\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{DIB}}(\mathcal{D}){} is harder for Bob (Prop. 3), but Alice’s prediction will improve (smaller minZ⁡minf∈𝒱⁡R​(f,Z)subscriptZsubscript𝑓𝒱R𝑓Z\min_{\mathrm{Z}}\min_{f\in\mathcal{V}}\mathrm{R}(f,\mathrm{Z}){}; theorem 1).

Case study: neural networks. Suppose that 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V} is a specific neural architecture, the encoder PZ|Xsubscript𝑃conditionalZXP_{\mathrm{Z}\,|\,\mathrm{X}} is parametrized by a neural network qθsubscript𝑞𝜃q_{\theta}, and we are interested in cat-dog classification. As shown in fig. 2(b), training qθsubscript𝑞𝜃q_{\theta} with DIB corresponds to fitting qθsubscript𝑞𝜃q_{\theta} with multiple classification heads, each having exactly the same architecture 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V} but different parameters. The 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-sufficiency head (in blue) tries to classify cats and dogs. Each of the K𝐾K (typically 3-4, see Sec. E.4) 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality heads (in orange) ensure that the representation cannot be used to classify an arbitrary (fixed) labeling of cats or dogs. In practice, the encoder and heads are trained jointly but gradients from 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality heads are reversed. The 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality losses are also multiplied by a hyper-parameter β𝛽\beta.

4 Experiments

We evaluate our framework in practical settings, focusing on: 1 the relation between 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-sufficiency and Alice’s best achievable performance; 2 the relation between 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality and generalization; 3 the consequence of a mismatch between 𝒱A​l​i​c​esubscript𝒱𝐴𝑙𝑖𝑐𝑒\mathcal{V}_{Alice} and the functional family 𝒱B​o​bsubscript𝒱𝐵𝑜𝑏\mathcal{V}_{Bob} w.r.t. which ZZ\mathrm{Z} is sufficient or minimal — especially in IB’s setting 𝒱B​o​b=𝒰subscript𝒱𝐵𝑜𝑏𝒰\mathcal{V}_{Bob}=\mathcal{U}{}; 4 the use of our framework to predict generalization of trained networks. Many of our experiments involve sweeping over the complexity of families 𝒱−⊆𝒱⊆𝒱+superscript𝒱𝒱superscript𝒱\mathcal{V}^{-}\subseteq\mathcal{V}\subseteq\mathcal{V}^{+}, we do this by varying widths of MLPs — with 𝒱→𝒰→𝒱𝒰\mathcal{V}\to\mathcal{U}{} in the infinite width limit [40, 41]. Alternative ways of sweeping over 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V} are evaluated in Sec. E.1.

4.1 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-sufficiency: Optimal Representations When the Data Distribution is Known

We study optimal representations when Alice has access to the data distribution PZ×Ysubscript𝑃ZYP_{\mathrm{Z}\times\mathrm{Y}}. Alice’s risk R​(f,Z)R𝑓Z\mathrm{R}(f,\mathrm{Z}){} in such setting is important as it is a tight lower bound on her performance in practical settings (see Sec. 3.1). We consider the following setting: Bob trains a ResNet18 encoder [42] by maximizing I𝒱Bob⁡[Z→Y]subscriptIsubscript𝒱Bob→ZY\operatorname{I_{\mathcal{V}_{Bob}}}\negthinspace\left[\mathrm{Z}\rightarrow\mathrm{Y}\right], Alice freezes it and trains her own classifier f∈𝒱A​l​i​c​e𝑓subscript𝒱𝐴𝑙𝑖𝑐𝑒f\in\mathcal{V}_{Alice} using the underlying PZ×Ysubscript𝑃ZYP_{\mathrm{Z}\times\mathrm{Y}}, i.e., f𝑓f is trained and evaluated on the same dataset. See Sec. D.1 for experimental details.

Which 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-sufficiency should Bob chose? Proposition 1 tells us that Bob’s optimal choice is 𝒱B​o​b=𝒱A​l​i​c​esubscript𝒱𝐵𝑜𝑏subscript𝒱𝐴𝑙𝑖𝑐𝑒\mathcal{V}_{Bob}=\mathcal{V}_{Alice}. If he opts for a larger family 𝒱A​l​i​c​e⊆𝒱B​o​bsubscript𝒱𝐴𝑙𝑖𝑐𝑒subscript𝒱𝐵𝑜𝑏\mathcal{V}_{Alice}\subseteq\mathcal{V}_{Bob}, the representation ZZ\mathrm{Z} is unlikely to be decodable by Alice. If 𝒱B​o​b⊆𝒱A​l​i​c​esubscript𝒱𝐵𝑜𝑏subscript𝒱𝐴𝑙𝑖𝑐𝑒\mathcal{V}_{Bob}\subseteq\mathcal{V}_{Alice}, he will unnecessarily constrain ZZ\mathrm{Z}. We first consider a setting that can be visualized: classifying the parity of CIFAR100 class index [43] using 2D representations. Figure 3(a) shows samples from ZZ\mathrm{Z} and Alice’s decision boundaries. To highlight the optimal 𝒱B​o​bsubscript𝒱𝐵𝑜𝑏\mathcal{V}_{Bob} for a given 𝒱A​l​i​c​esubscript𝒱𝐴𝑙𝑖𝑐𝑒\mathcal{V}_{Alice}, we scale the performance of each column from 00 to 100100100 in the figure. As predicted by Prop. 1, the best performance is achieved at 𝒱A​l​i​c​e=𝒱B​o​bsubscript𝒱𝐴𝑙𝑖𝑐𝑒subscript𝒱𝐵𝑜𝑏\mathcal{V}_{Alice}=\mathcal{V}_{Bob}. The worst predictions arise when 𝒱A​l​i​c​e⊆𝒱B​o​bsubscript𝒱𝐴𝑙𝑖𝑐𝑒subscript𝒱𝐵𝑜𝑏\mathcal{V}_{Alice}\subseteq\mathcal{V}_{Bob}, as the representations cannot be separated by Alice’s classifier (e.g. 𝒱B​o​bsubscript𝒱𝐵𝑜𝑏\mathcal{V}_{Bob} width 16 and 𝒱A​l​i​c​esubscript𝒱𝐴𝑙𝑖𝑐𝑒\mathcal{V}_{Alice} width 1). This suggests that IB’s sufficiency (infinite width 𝒱B​o​b=𝒰subscript𝒱𝐵𝑜𝑏𝒰\mathcal{V}_{Bob}=\mathcal{U}{}) is undesirable when 𝒱A​l​i​c​esubscript𝒱𝐴𝑙𝑖𝑐𝑒\mathcal{V}_{Alice} is constrained. Figure 3(b) shows similar results in 8D across 5 runs. See Sec. E.8 for more settings.

4.2 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality: Optimal Representations for Generalization

Theorem 1 states that 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality ensures all ERMs can generalize well. We investigate whether this is still approximately the case in practical settings, i.e., when Bob optimizes ℒ^DIB​(𝒟)subscript^ℒDIB𝒟\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{DIB}}(\mathcal{D}){}.

Experimental Details. Our claim concerns all ERMs 𝒱^∗​(𝒟)superscript^𝒱𝒟\hat{\mathcal{V}}^{*}(\mathcal{D}), which cannot be supported by training a few f^∈𝒱^∗​(𝒟)^𝑓superscript^𝒱𝒟\hat{f}{}\in\hat{\mathcal{V}}^{*}(\mathcal{D}). Instead, we evaluate the ERM that performs worst on the test set (Worst ERM), i.e., arg⁡maxf∈𝒱^∗​(𝒟)⁡R​(f,Z)subscript𝑓superscript^𝒱𝒟R𝑓Z\arg\max_{f\in\hat{\mathcal{V}}^{*}(\mathcal{D})}\mathrm{R}(f,\mathrm{Z}){}. We do so by optimizing the following Lagrangian relaxation arg⁡minf∈𝒱⁡R^​(f,Z;𝒟)−γ​R​(f,Z)subscript𝑓𝒱^R𝑓Z𝒟𝛾R𝑓Z\arg\min_{f\in\mathcal{V}}\hat{\mathrm{R}}(f,\mathrm{Z};\mathcal{D}){}-\gamma\mathrm{R}(f,\mathrm{Z}){} (see Sec. E.7). As our theory does not impose constraints on ZZ\mathrm{Z}, we need an encoder close to a universal function approximator. We use a 3-MLP encoder with around 21M parameters and a 1024 dimensional ZZ\mathrm{Z}. Since we want to investigate the generalization of ERMs resulting from Bob’s criterion, we do not use (possibly implicit) regularizers such as large learning rate [44]. For more experimental details see Sec. D.1.

What is the impact of DIB’s β𝛽\beta ? We train representions on CIFAR10 with various β𝛽\beta to investigate the effect of I^𝒱⁡[Z→Dec​(X,𝒴);𝒟]subscript^I𝒱→ZDecX𝒴𝒟\operatorname{\hat{I}_{\mathcal{V}}}\negthinspace\left[\mathrm{Z}\rightarrow\mathrm{Dec}(\mathrm{X},\mathcal{Y}){};\mathcal{D}\right]{} and I^𝒱⁡[Y→Z;𝒟]subscript^I𝒱→YZ𝒟\operatorname{\hat{I}_{\mathcal{V}}}\negthinspace\left[\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow\mathrm{Z};\mathcal{D}\right] (fig. 4(b)) on Alice’s performance (fig. 4(a)). Increasing β𝛽\beta results in a decrease in I^𝒱⁡[Z→Dec​(X,𝒴);𝒟]subscript^I𝒱→ZDecX𝒴𝒟\operatorname{\hat{I}_{\mathcal{V}}}\negthinspace\left[\mathrm{Z}\rightarrow\mathrm{Dec}(\mathrm{X},\mathcal{Y}){};\mathcal{D}\right]{} which monotonically shrinks the train-test gap. This suggests that, although our theory only applies for 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality, I𝒱⁡[Z→Dec​(X,𝒴)]subscriptI𝒱→ZDecX𝒴\operatorname{I_{\mathcal{V}}}\negthinspace\left[\mathrm{Z}\rightarrow\mathrm{Dec}(\mathrm{X},\mathcal{Y}){}\right]{} is tightly linked to generalization even when it is non-zero. After a certain threshold (β=10𝛽10\beta=10) the generalization gains come at a large cost in I𝒱⁡[Y→Z]subscriptI𝒱→YZ\operatorname{I_{\mathcal{V}}}\negthinspace\left[\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow\mathrm{Z}\right], which controls the best achievable loss. This shows that a trade-off (controlled by β𝛽\beta) between 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality (generalization) and 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-sufficient (lower bound) arises when Bob has to estimate ℒDIBsubscriptℒDIB\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DIB}}{} using finite samples ℒ^DIB​(𝒟)subscript^ℒDIB𝒟\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{DIB}}(\mathcal{D}){}.

𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality and robustness to spurious correlations. We overlay MNIST digits as a distractor on CIFAR10 (see Sec. D.2). We run the same experiments as with CIFAR10, but we additionally train an ERM from 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V} to predict MNIST labels, i.e., test whether ZZ\mathrm{Z} contains decodable information about MNIST. Figure 4(c) shows that as β𝛽\beta increases, predicting MNIST becomes harder. Indeed decreasing I^𝒱⁡[Z→Dec​(X,𝒴);𝒟]subscript^I𝒱→ZDecX𝒴𝒟\operatorname{\hat{I}_{\mathcal{V}}}\negthinspace\left[\mathrm{Z}\rightarrow\mathrm{Dec}(\mathrm{X},\mathcal{Y}){};\mathcal{D}\right]{} removes all 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-information in ZZ\mathrm{Z} which is not useful for predicting YY\mathrm{Y}. As a result, Alice’s ERM must generalize better as it cannot over-fit spurious patterns.777Achille and Soatto [20] show that this happens for minimal ZZ\mathrm{Z}. The novelty is that we obtain similar results when considering 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality, which is less stringent (Prop. 2) and does not require the intractable I⁡[X;Z]IXZ\operatorname{I}\negthinspace\left[\mathrm{X};\mathrm{Z}\right].

Which 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality should Bob chose? We study the effect of Z∈𝒮𝒱A​l​i​c​eZsubscript𝒮subscript𝒱𝐴𝑙𝑖𝑐𝑒\mathrm{Z}\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{V}_{Alice}} being minimal w.r.t. families which are larger (𝒱+superscript𝒱\mathcal{V}^{+}-DIB), smaller (𝒱−superscript𝒱\mathcal{V}^{-}-DIB), and equal to 𝒱A​l​i​c​esubscript𝒱𝐴𝑙𝑖𝑐𝑒\mathcal{V}_{Alice}. In theory, optimal representations would be 𝒱A​l​i​c​esubscript𝒱𝐴𝑙𝑖𝑐𝑒\mathcal{V}_{Alice}-minimal (Theorem 1), which are achieved by DIB and 𝒱+superscript𝒱\mathcal{V}^{+}-DIB (Monotonicity). 𝒱+superscript𝒱\mathcal{V}^{+}-DIB should nevertheless be harder to estimate than DIB (Prop. 3). In the last 3 columns of table 1 we indeed observe that DIB performs best. 𝒱+superscript𝒱\mathcal{V}^{+}-DIB performs worse, suggesting that IB’s minimality is undesirable in practice. We also minimize a known lower bound of I⁡[Z;X]IZX\operatorname{I}\negthinspace\left[\mathrm{Z};\mathrm{X}\right] (VIB; [19]) and find that it performs worse than DIB.888 VIB is hard to compare to DIB as it is unclear w.r.t. which family, if any, VIB’s solutions are minimal. We show results for different β𝛽\beta in Sec. E.10.

Comparison to traditional regularizers. To ensure that the previous experimental gains support our theory and are not necessarily true for other regularizers, we test different regularizers on Bob and see whether they also learn representations that ensure Alice’s ERM will generalize. In table 1, we show the results of: 1 No regularization; 2 Stochastic representations (DIB with β=0𝛽0\beta=0); 3 Dropout [45]; 4 Weight decay. We find that DIB significantly outperforms other regularizers, which supports our claims that 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality is well-suited for enforcing generalization. We emphasize that we evaluate the regularizers in a setting which is closer to our theory: two-stage game, no implicit regularizers, and evaluated on log likelihood. We show in Sec. E.11 that DIB is a descent regularizer in standard classification settings but performs a little worse than dropout.

4.3 Probing Generalization in Deep Learning

Methods that predict or correlate with the generalization of neural networks have been of recent theoretical and practical interest [46, 47, 48, 49, 50, 51], as they can shed light on the inductive biases in deep learning [52, 53, 54] and prescribe better training procedures [55, 56, 57, 58, 59]. Having empirically shown a strong link between the degree of 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality and generalization (fig. 2(b)), it is natural to ask whether it can predict the generalization of a trained model. Specifically, consider the first L𝐿L layers as an encoder from inputs XX\mathrm{X} to representations ZLsubscriptZ𝐿\mathrm{Z}_{L}, and subsequent layers as a classifier in 𝒱Lsubscript𝒱𝐿\mathcal{V}_{L}. We hypothesize that I^𝒱L⁡[ZL→Dec​(X,𝒴);𝒟]subscript^Isubscript𝒱L→subscriptZ𝐿DecX𝒴𝒟\operatorname{\hat{I}_{\mathcal{V}_{L}}}\negthinspace\left[\mathrm{Z}_{L}\rightarrow\mathrm{Dec}(\mathrm{X},\mathcal{Y}){};\mathcal{D}\right] correlates well with the generalization of the network.

To test this, we follow Jiang et al. [50] and train convolutional networks (CNN) with varying hyperparameters (depth, width, dropout, batch size, weight decay, learning rate, dimensionality of ZZ\mathrm{Z}) and retain those that reach 0.010.010.01 empirical risk. From this set of 562 models, we measure Kendall’s rank correlation [60] between I^𝒱L⁡[ZL→Dec​(X,𝒴);𝒟]subscript^Isubscript𝒱L→subscriptZ𝐿DecX𝒴𝒟\operatorname{\hat{I}_{\mathcal{V}_{L}}}\negthinspace\left[\mathrm{Z}_{L}\rightarrow\mathrm{Dec}(\mathrm{X},\mathcal{Y}){};\mathcal{D}\right] and the generalization gap of each CNN, i.e., the difference between their train and test performance. For experimental details see Sec. D.3.

Does 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality correlate with generalization? In the last five columns of table 2, we compare our results (𝒱Lsubscript𝒱𝐿\mathcal{V}_{L}) to the best generalization measure from each categories investigated in [50]: the entropy of the output [61], the path norm [62], the variance of the gradients after training (Var. Grad. ; [50]), and the “sharpness” of the minima (Sharp. Mag.; [57]).999 We report Jiang et al.’s [50] results since our experiments and Sharp. Mag. differs slightly from theirs. As hypothesized, I^𝒱L⁡[ZL→Dec​(X,𝒴);𝒟]subscript^Isubscript𝒱L→subscriptZ𝐿DecX𝒴𝒟\operatorname{\hat{I}_{\mathcal{V}_{L}}}\negthinspace\left[\mathrm{Z}_{L}\rightarrow\mathrm{Dec}(\mathrm{X},\mathcal{Y}){};\mathcal{D}\right] correlates with generalization and even outperforms the baselines. Similarly to table 1 we also evaluate minimality with respect to a family larger (𝒱L+superscriptsubscript𝒱𝐿\mathcal{V}_{L}^{+}) or smaller (𝒱L−superscriptsubscript𝒱𝐿\mathcal{V}_{L}^{-}) than 𝒱Lsubscript𝒱𝐿\mathcal{V}_{L}. Surprisingly, 𝒱L+superscriptsubscript𝒱𝐿\mathcal{V}_{L}^{+} performs better than 𝒱Lsubscript𝒱𝐿\mathcal{V}_{L}, which might be because larger networks can help optimization of sub-networks 𝒱L⊆𝒱L+subscript𝒱𝐿superscriptsubscript𝒱𝐿\mathcal{V}_{L}\subseteq\mathcal{V}_{L}^{+} as suggested by the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis [63].

To the best of our knowledge 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality is the first measure of generalization of a network that only considers a single internal representation ZLsubscriptZ𝐿\mathrm{Z}_{L}. This could be of particular interest in transfer learning, as it can predict how well any model of a certain architecture will generalize when using a specific pretrained encoder. As 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality is a property of a representation rather than the architecture, we show in Sec. E.12 that it can be meaningfully compared across different architectures and datasets.

5 Other Related Work

Generalized information, game theory and Bayes decision theory. If you need a distribution PX∗subscriptsuperscript𝑃XP^{*}_{\mathrm{X}} to act as a representative Γ⊆𝒫​(𝒳)Γ𝒫𝒳\Gamma\subseteq\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X}) you should follow the maximum entropy (MaxEnt) principle [64, 65] to minimize the worst-case log loss [66, 67]. Grünwald et al. [68] generalized MaxEnt to different losses by framing the problem as an adversarial game between nature and a decision maker. Robust supervised learning [69] can also be framed in a way that suggests to maximize conditional entropy [70, 71]. This line of work focuses on prediction rules (Alice). Our framing (Sec. 2.1) extends this literature by incorporating a co-operative agent (Bob), which learns representations to minimize the worst-case loss of the decision maker (Alice). Although [72, 10] also studied representations using generalized information, they focused on consistency rather than generalization.

Extended sufficiency and minimality. Linear sufficiency is well studied [73, 74, 75] but only considers linear encoders and predictors and is used for estimation rather than predictions. In ML, Cvitkovic and Koliander [76] incorporated the encoder’s family (Bob) to characterize achievable ZZ\mathrm{Z}. This is complementary to our incorporation of the decoder’s family 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V} (Alice) to characterize optimal ZZ\mathrm{Z}.

Kernel Learning. There is a large literature in learning kernels [77, 78, 79, 80] for support vector machines [2], which implicitly learns a data representation [81]. The learning is either done by minimizing estimates [82, 83] or bounds of the generalization error [84, 85, 86, 87, 88]. The major advantage of our work is that we are not restricted to predictors 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V} that can be “kernelized” and provide an optimality proof.

6 Conclusion and Future Work

In this work, we propose a prescriptive theory for representation learning. We first characterize optimal representations Z∗superscriptZ\mathrm{Z}^{*} for supervised learning, by defining minimal sufficient representation with respect to a family of classifiers 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}. These representations Z∗superscriptZ\mathrm{Z}^{*} guarantee that any downstream empirical risk minimizer f∈𝒱𝑓𝒱f\in\mathcal{V} will incur minimal expected test loss, by ensuring that f𝑓f can correctly predict labels but cannot distinguish examples with the same label. We then provide the decodable information bottleneck objective to learn Z∗superscriptZ\mathrm{Z}^{*} with PAC-style guarantees. We empirically show that using Z∗superscriptZ\mathrm{Z}^{*} can improve the performance and robustness of image classifiers. We also demonstrate that our framework can be used to predict generalization in neural networks.

In addition to supporting our theory, our experiments raise interesting questions for future work. First, results in Sec. 4.2 suggest that performance is causally related with the degree of 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality of a representation, even though we only prove it for “perfect” 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality. A natural question, then, is whether generalization bounds can be derived for approximate 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality. Second, the high correlation between generalization in neural networks and the degree 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality (table 2) suggest that it might be an important quantity to study for understanding generalization in deep learning.

More generally, our work shows that information theory in theoretical and applied ML can benefit from incorporating the predictive family 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V} of interest. For example, we believe that many issues of mutual information [89] in self-supervised learning [90, 91, 92], and IB [93, 94, 33] in IB’s theory of deep learning [95, 14] could be solved by taking into account 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}. By extending 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-information to arbitrary r.v. (through decompositions) we hope to enable its use in those and many other domains.

Broader Impact

Our work takes the perspective that an “optimal” representation is one such that any classifier that fits the training data should generalize well to test. In terms of potential practical benefits, it is possible that using our optimal representations, one can alleviate the effort of hyperparameter search and selection currently required to tune deep learning models. This could be a step towards democratizing machine learning to sections of the society without large computational resources – since hyperparameter search is often computationally expensive. We do not anticipate that our work will advantage or disadvantage any particular group.

In the following appendices we: 1 Formalize our notation in Appx. A; 2 State and discuss our assumptions in Appx. B; 3 State and prove our theoretical results in Appx. C; 4 Provide details for reproducing our results in Appx. D; 5 Provide and discuss additional results that shed light on many of our design choices Appx. E.

Appendix B Assumptions

B.1 Generic Assumptions

We make a some assumptions throughout our paper to have concise statements. First let us discuss generic assumptions about the setting we are studying:

At least one example per class

We assume that every training set has at least one example per label. This is generally true in modern ML, where |𝒟|≫|𝒴|much-greater-than𝒟𝒴|\mathcal{D}|\gg|\mathcal{Y}|. Theorem 1 would not hold without it, as ERMs could not perform optimally without having examples to learn from.

Logarithmic score

We only consider the log loss S​(y,f​[z])≔−log⁡f​[z]​(y)≔𝑆𝑦𝑓delimited-[]𝑧𝑓delimited-[]𝑧𝑦S(y,f[z])\coloneqq-\log f[z](y) as it is the most common scoring rule. Indeed, it is (essentially) the only strictly proper (strictly minimized by the underlying distribution PY×Zsubscript𝑃YZP_{\mathrm{Y}\times\mathrm{Z}}) and local (depending only on predicted probability of the observed event PY×Z​(y|Z)subscript𝑃YZconditional𝑦ZP_{\mathrm{Y}\times\mathrm{Z}}(y|\mathrm{Z})) scoring rule [96], making it computationally attractive. The framework can likely be extended to any proper scoring rule (e.g. pseudo-likelihood, Brier score, kernel scoring rule) by considering generalized predictive entropy [97, 68, 34].

Finite sample spaces

We restrict ourselves to finite |𝒳|𝒳|\mathcal{X}|,|𝒴|𝒴|\mathcal{Y}|,|𝒵|𝒵|\mathcal{Z}|, so as to avoid the use of measure theory and axiomatic set theory, which would obscure the main points of the paper. While this assumption holds in computational ML (due to the use of digital computer or the fact that we can always restrict the sample spaces to the finite examples seen in our training and testing set), it is unsatisfactory from a theoretical standpoint and the general case should be investigated in future work. We conjecture that theorem 1 extends to the uncountable case.

At least as many representations as labels

The sample space of representions is at least as large as the one for labels: |𝒵|≥|𝒴|𝒵𝒴|\mathcal{Z}|\geq|\mathcal{Y}|. This holds in practice where there are usually less than a 1000 possible labels 𝒴𝒴\mathcal{Y} while even a single dimensional ZZ\mathrm{Z} can often (depending on computer) take 232≈4∗106superscript2324superscript1062^{32}\approx 4*10^{6} values.

Multi-class classification

The sample space of the target is 𝒴=[0,…,|𝒴|−1]𝒴0…𝒴1\mathcal{Y}=[0,\dots,|\mathcal{Y}|-1].

B.2 Assumptions on Functional Families

Now let us discuss the assumptions that we make about functional families. The following assumptions hold for many functional families that are used in practice, including neural networks, logistic regression, and decision tree classifiers.

Invariance of 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V} to label permutations

All predictive families are invariant to permutation, i.e., ∀𝒱,∀π:𝒴→𝒴:for-all𝒱for-all𝜋→𝒴𝒴\forall\mathcal{V},\ \forall\pi:\mathcal{Y}\to\mathcal{Y}, ∀f∈𝒱,∃f′∈𝒱formulae-sequencefor-all𝑓𝒱superscript𝑓′𝒱\forall f\in\mathcal{V},\ \exists f^{\prime}\in\mathcal{V} s.t. ∀z∈𝒵,∀y∈𝒴formulae-sequencefor-all𝑧𝒵for-all𝑦𝒴\forall z\in\mathcal{Z},\forall y\in\mathcal{Y} we have ∀f​[z]​(y)=f′​[z]​(π​(y))for-all𝑓delimited-[]𝑧𝑦superscript𝑓′delimited-[]𝑧𝜋𝑦\forall f[z](y)=f^{\prime}[z](\pi(y)). This holds in practice (neural networks, decision trees, …) as we usually do not want predictors to depend on the order of labels, e.g. 𝒴={`​`​c​a​t​",`​`​d​o​g​"}𝒴``𝑐𝑎𝑡"``𝑑𝑜𝑔"\mathcal{Y}=\{``cat",``dog"\} or 𝒴={`​`​d​o​g​",`​`​c​a​t​"}𝒴``𝑑𝑜𝑔"``𝑐𝑎𝑡"\mathcal{Y}=\{``dog",``cat"\}. We use this assumption to simplify the proof of theorem 1.

Non-empty preimage of labels

We consider predictive families that have a non empty preimage for each label: ∀𝒱for-all𝒱\forall\mathcal{V}, ∃f∈𝒱𝑓𝒱\exists f\in\mathcal{V}, s.t. ∀y∈𝒴,∃z∈𝒵formulae-sequencefor-all𝑦𝒴𝑧𝒵\forall y\in\mathcal{Y},\ \exists z\in\mathcal{Z} we have f​[z]​(y)=1𝑓delimited-[]𝑧𝑦1f[z](y)=1. This is usually true in ML. In neural networks, this can be achieved by making the weights of your last layer very large such that the softmax will give the label a probability of 1 (achieved due to floating point representation). We use this assumption to show that when the label is deterministic, R∗​(𝒱)=0superscriptR𝒱0\mathrm{R}^{*}(\mathcal{V})=0.

Arbitrary constant prediction of 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}

We assume that in all functional families there always is a predictor which predicts any constant output regardless of the input: ∀𝒱,∀PY∈𝒫​(𝒴),∃f∈𝒱formulae-sequencefor-all𝒱for-allsubscript𝑃Y𝒫𝒴𝑓𝒱\forall\mathcal{V},\ \forall P_{\mathrm{Y}}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y}),\ \exists f\in\mathcal{V} s.t. ∀z∈𝒵for-all𝑧𝒵\forall z\in\mathcal{Z} we have f​[z]=PY𝑓delimited-[]𝑧subscript𝑃Yf[z]=P_{\mathrm{Y}}. This is typically true in classification, when the last layer parametrizes a categorical distribution. In neural networks this can be achieved by setting all weights to 00 and then the bias of the last layer (softmax) to the desired values. Notice that this not true in the general case (regression and countable infinite sample space), in which case the assumption can be relaxed to optional ignorance as in [23]. We use this assumption to simplify the definition of 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-information in Prop. 5.

Monotonic biasing of 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}

We assume that all functional families are closed under “monotonic biasing towards a prediction y𝑦y”. Formally, ∀f′∈𝒱,∀y∈𝒴,∀z∈𝒵,∀p∈[0,1]formulae-sequencefor-allsuperscript𝑓′𝒱formulae-sequencefor-all𝑦𝒴formulae-sequencefor-all𝑧𝒵for-all𝑝01\forall f^{\prime}\in\mathcal{V},\ \forall y\in\mathcal{Y},\ \forall z\in\mathcal{Z},\ \forall p\in[0,1], ∃g∈𝒱𝑔𝒱\exists g\in\mathcal{V} s.t. g​[z]​(y)=p𝑔delimited-[]𝑧𝑦𝑝g[z](y)=p and ∀z′,z′′∈𝒵,∀y′∈𝒴formulae-sequencefor-allsuperscript𝑧′superscript𝑧′′𝒵for-allsuperscript𝑦′𝒴\forall z^{\prime},z^{\prime\prime}\in\mathcal{Z},\forall y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y} we have sign​(f′​[z′]​(y′)−f′​[z′′]​(y′))=sign​(g​[z′]​(y′)−g​[z′′]​(y′))signsuperscript𝑓′delimited-[]superscript𝑧′superscript𝑦′superscript𝑓′delimited-[]superscript𝑧′′superscript𝑦′sign𝑔delimited-[]superscript𝑧′superscript𝑦′𝑔delimited-[]superscript𝑧′′superscript𝑦′\mathrm{sign}(f^{\prime}[z^{\prime}](y^{\prime})-f^{\prime}[z^{\prime\prime}](y^{\prime}))=\mathrm{sign}(g[z^{\prime}](y^{\prime})-g[z^{\prime\prime}](y^{\prime})). In other words, it is possible to construct a g∈𝒱𝑔𝒱g\in\mathcal{V} that assigns to a (single) pair z,y𝑧𝑦z,y the probability p𝑝p of your choice and preserves the order — if z,y𝑧𝑦z,y was assigned a higher probability than z′,ysuperscript𝑧′𝑦z^{\prime},y by f′superscript𝑓′f^{\prime} then the same holds for g𝑔g. Such assumption holds for neural networks, as it is always possible to construct g𝑔g by modifying the bias term of the final softmax layer. This assumption is crucial for the proof of theorem 1.

B.3 Assumptions for the Theorem

We make an additional assumptions for theorem 1 and Prop. 2.

Deterministic Labeling

We assume that labels are deterministic functions of the data ∃t:𝒳→𝒴:𝑡→𝒳𝒴\exists t:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y} s.t. Y=t​(X)Y𝑡X\mathrm{Y}=t(\mathrm{X}). This is generally true in ML datasets where every example is only seen once and thus every example is given a single label with probability 1. This does not necessarily hold in the real world. We use this assumption to simplify the proofs, we believe that it is not necessary for the theorem to hold but should be investigated in future work.

Appendix C Theoretical Results and Proofs

C.1 Background

C.1.1 Minimal Sufficient Statistics

In the following, we clarify the link between minimal sufficient statistics [25] and representations [12, 24] of inputs XX\mathrm{X}. The difference between a representation ZZ\mathrm{Z} in IB and a statistic T​(X)𝑇XT(\mathrm{X}), is that the mapping between the inputs XX\mathrm{X} and the representation ZZ\mathrm{Z} can be stochastic — specifically a representation is a statistic of the input and independent noise ϵ⟂Xperpendicular-toitalic-ϵX\epsilon\perp\mathrm{X}, i.e., Z=T​(X,ϵ)Z𝑇Xitalic-ϵ\mathrm{Z}=T(\mathrm{X},\epsilon). We now prove that for (deterministic) statistics, the notion of minimal sufficient representation is equivalent to that of predictive minimal sufficient statistics [98].

A representation Z=T​(X,ϵ)Z𝑇Xitalic-ϵ\mathrm{Z}=T(\mathrm{X},\epsilon) is:

Appendix D Reproducibility

In this section we provide further details of the hyperparameters chosen for the various experiments in the main text. Unless stated otherwise, all the models are trained for 300 epochs, using Adam [99] as the optimizer, a learning rate of 5​e−55𝑒55e-5, at every epoch we decay all learning rates by (1/100)(1/300)superscript11001300(1/100)^{(1/300)} (so that the learning rate is decayed by 100100100 during the entire training), a batch-size of 256, without data augmentation, and using 5 and 3 random seeds respectively for experiments in the main text and appendices. We checkpoint and use the model which achieves the smallest training loss for evaluation.131313Notice that we use a small learning rate, a large number of epochs, and checkpoint based on training loss because we are interested in studying the generalization ability of a model depending solely on the criterion being optimized over. Activation functions are LeakyReLU​(x)=max⁡(x,0.01∗x)LeakyReLU𝑥𝑥0.01𝑥\mathrm{LeakyReLU}(x)=\max(x,0.01*x) while other unspecified parameters are PyTorch [100] defaults. The code can also be found at github.com/YannDubs/Mini_Decodable_Information_Bottleneck.

D.1 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-Minimality 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-Sufficiency

Bob’s encoder is a neural network which maps the input XX\mathrm{X} to a mean μzsubscript𝜇𝑧\mu_{z} and standard deviation σzsubscript𝜎𝑧\sigma_{z} used to parametrize a multivariate normal distribution with diagonal Gaussian: PZ|X=𝒩​(Z;μz,softplus​(σz−5))subscript𝑃conditionalZX𝒩Zsubscript𝜇𝑧softplussubscript𝜎𝑧5P_{\mathrm{Z}|\mathrm{X}}=\mathcal{N}(\mathrm{Z};\mu_{z},\mathrm{softplus}(\sigma_{z}-5)), where softplus​(⋅)=log⁡(1+exp⁡(⋅))softplus⋅1⋅\mathrm{softplus}(\cdot)=\log(1+\exp(\cdot)). Note that we use −55-5 as done in VIB [19] to make the methods more comparable. During training we sample a single z∼PZ|Xsimilar-to𝑧subscript𝑃conditionalZXz\sim P_{\mathrm{Z}|\mathrm{X}}, while we sample 12 during evaluation (as done in VIB [19]). 141414Contrary to VIB, DIB does not require the use of an encoder that parameterizes a Gaussian distribution. We use a Gaussian to make it more comparable to VIB. The representation then goes through a batch normalization layer without trainable parameters (setting the mean to 0 and standard deviation to 1), which ensures that the representation cannot diverge as discussed in Sec. E.3.

The encoder is trained using two losses which are weighted by a hyperparameter β𝛽\beta, ℒ^DIB​(𝒟)=ℒ𝒱​suff−β​ℒ𝒱​minsubscript^ℒDIB𝒟subscriptℒ𝒱suff𝛽subscriptℒ𝒱min\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{DIB}}(\mathcal{D}){}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{V}\text{suff}}-\beta\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{V}\text{min}}:

  • •

    𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-sufficiency ℒ𝒱​suffsubscriptℒ𝒱suff\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{V}\text{suff}}. The representation z𝑧z goes through a head of architecture 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}. The last layer of this head goes through a softmax to parametrize a distribution over of labels, i.e., f​[z]​(y)𝑓delimited-[]𝑧𝑦f[z](y) corresponds to the yt​hsuperscript𝑦𝑡ℎy^{th} neuron in that layer. The resulting loss ℒ𝒱​suffsubscriptℒ𝒱suff\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{V}\text{suff}} is the standard cross entropy. We then back-propagate to jointly minimize the loss with respect to the head and the encoder.

  • •

    𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality ℒ𝒱​minsubscriptℒ𝒱min\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{V}\text{min}}. In addition to being used for ℒ𝒱​suffsubscriptℒ𝒱suff\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{V}\text{suff}}, the representation z𝑧z is used as input to 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality heads that each predict a different N∈Dec​(X,y)NDecX𝑦\mathrm{N}\in\mathrm{Dec}(\mathrm{X},y){} in the same way as how the 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-sufficiency head predicts the label YY\mathrm{Y}. We get each NN\mathrm{N} using algorithm 1, i.e., assigning each example x∈𝒳𝑥𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} some index and then performing base |𝒴|𝒴|\mathcal{Y}| expansion (see Sec. E.5). For the case of CIFAR10 this corresponds to: 1 assigning each image some index between 00 and the number of examples (∼6000similar-toabsent6000\sim 6000); 2 having 4 nuisance labels NN\mathrm{N} corresponding to each digit of the new index, e.g., the cat number 627 will have N1=0subscriptN10\mathrm{N}_{1}=0, N2=6subscriptN26\mathrm{N}_{2}=6, N3=2subscriptN32\mathrm{N}_{3}=2, N4=7subscriptN47\mathrm{N}_{4}=7 .

    Each 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality head predicts the corresponding NN\mathrm{N}. Having to treat every example differently based on their underlying label y𝑦y (“for loop” in fig. 2(a)) is not amenable to batch GPU training, which assumes that every example in a batch is treated the same way. We thus use the same predictor for a set {Dec​(X,y)}y∈𝒴subscriptDecX𝑦𝑦𝒴\{\mathrm{Dec}(\mathrm{X},y){}\}_{y\in\mathcal{Y}} (see Sec. E.6), i.e., instead of having one predictor for Dec​(X,cat)DecXcat\mathrm{Dec}(\mathrm{X},\text{cat}) and another for Dec​(X,dog)DecXdog\mathrm{Dec}(\mathrm{X},\text{dog}) where representations are z∼Zysimilar-to𝑧subscriptZ𝑦z\sim\mathrm{Z}_{y} (as shown in Appx. D) we use a single head to predict both Dec​(X,cat),Dec​(X,dog)DecXcatDecXdog\mathrm{Dec}(\mathrm{X},\text{cat}),\mathrm{Dec}(\mathrm{X},\text{dog}) using representations z∈Z𝑧Zz\in\mathrm{Z} from cats or dogs as inputs. By taking an average over the loss of each head we get the ℒ𝒱​minsubscriptℒ𝒱min\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{V}\text{min}} term of fig. 2(a). Throughout the paper we unroll the optimization of 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality heads for 5 steps, i.e., for every batch ℒ𝒱​min)\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{V}\text{min}}) is minimized by 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality heads while the encoder maximizes it. We show in Sec. E.2 that, as seen in fig. 2(b), DIB can perform similarly well with joint gradient ascent descent — by reversing gradients which is more efficient and easier to implement.

Once the encoder is trained, we can train Alice’s classifier by:

  • •

    Standard (Avg, ERM). We freeze the trained encoder and use the representations as inputs to Alices head of architecture 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}. Alice then trains her classifier by minimizing the usual cross-entropy.

  • •

    Worst ERM. In some cases we want to explicitly find a Classifier from Alice that will perform well on train but bad on test. To do so, we optimize arg⁡minf∈V⁡R^​(f,Z;𝒟)−0.1∗R​(f,Z)subscript𝑓𝑉^R𝑓Z𝒟0.1R𝑓Z\arg\min_{f\in V}\hat{\mathrm{R}}(f,\mathrm{Z};\mathcal{D}){}-0.1*\mathrm{R}(f,\mathrm{Z}){} (see Sec. E.7), which corresponds to minimizing the training cross-entropy while directly maximizing the test cross-entropy.

Finally, Alice’s classifier is then evaluated by its test log loss (risk).

D.1.1 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-Sufficiency

For the 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-Sufficiency experiments (Sec. 4.1), we use a ResNet18 for Bob’s encoder and a single-hidden layer MLP for Alice with varying width (see Sec. E.1 for details and justification). For fig. 3(a) we use a 2 dimensional ZZ\mathrm{Z} and odd-even classification of CIFAR100. For fig. 3(b) we use a 8 dimensional ZZ\mathrm{Z} and full CIFAR100. The encoder is trained to be 𝒱B​o​bsubscript𝒱𝐵𝑜𝑏\mathcal{V}_{Bob}-sufficient and so we do do not use ℒ𝒱​minsubscriptℒ𝒱min\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{V}\text{min}}. Alice uses an architecture 𝒱A​l​i​c​esubscript𝒱𝐴𝑙𝑖𝑐𝑒\mathcal{V}_{Alice} and is trained using standard cross-entropy. To support Prop. 1 we want to show that 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-sufficient representations are optimal when Bob and Alice have access to the entire underlying distribution. As a result, we evaluate Alice’s classifier on the training set.

D.1.2 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-Minimality 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-Sufficiency

For the 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality experiments (Sec. 4.2), our goal is to show that if Bob trains 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimal 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-sufficient representations, any ERM trained by Alice will perform well on test (supporting theorem 1).

Since our theory does not impose any limitation on the possible representations ZZ\mathrm{Z}, we need an encoder that is very flexible and as close as possible to a universal function approximator. Thus, we use a large MLP with three hidden layers each with 2048 hidden units, for a total of around 21M parameters. Furthermore, we use a 1024 dimensional ZZ\mathrm{Z} in order to avoid constraints arising from a dimensionality bottleneck rather than from the criterion that Bob uses to train ZZ\mathrm{Z}. Alice’s predictive family 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V} is a single hidden layer MLP with 128 hidden units. As the encoder is much larger than 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V} we increase the learning rate of 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality heads by a factor of 505050 to make sure that they can “keep up” with the changing encoder.

For fig. 4(a) and fig. 4(b) (Effect of DIB on generalization), we use the CIFAR10 dataset, and train Alice’s classifier in the “Worst ERM” setting. The same holds for fig. 4(c), but uses the CIFAR10+MNIST dataset (see Sec. D.2). In this case, the Bob’s encoder is still trained using only CIFAR10. Once the encoder is trained and frozen, we evaluate how well Alice’s (worst) ERM can predict the CIFAR10 labels (as before). In addition, we also train another classifier in 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V} to predict the MNIST labels, using the same encoder.

For table 1 (performance of Avg. and worst ERM for different regularizers) we train the encoder in different ways, and Alice’s classifier in the “Worst ERM” (top row) and “Avg. ERM” (bottom row) settings. Importantly, each regularizer is used only during Bob’s training, as we are interested to know how DIB performs compared to other regularizers for representation learning, when the Alice’s downstream classifier is an empirical risk minimizer as in our problem formulation (Sec. 2.1). The regularizers are as follows (we tuned all models): 1 “No Reg.” does not use any regularizer and the encoder directly outputs the representation z𝑧z rather than a distribution from which to sample (this is the only such deterministic encoder in these results); 2 “Stoch Rep.” does not use any regularizer but the encoder is the same as the one used in DIB, i.e., it parametrizes a Gaussian distribution from which 12 z𝑧z are sampled and the predictions are marginalized over these samples; 3 “Dropout” uses 50% dropout after every layer in the encoder and is kept when training Alice’s encoder; 4 “Wt. Dec.” uses 1e-4 weight decay during Bob’s training; 5 “VIB” uses a KL-divergence “regularizer” to force the parametrized to be closer to a standard normal distribution (as described in [19]), the weight of the regularizer β=1​e−1𝛽1𝑒1\beta=1e-1. 6 “𝒱−superscript𝒱\mathcal{V}^{-}-DIB” uses a one hidden layer MLP with 2 hidden units (instead of 128) and β=100𝛽100\beta=100. 7 “𝒱+superscript𝒱\mathcal{V}^{+}-DIB” uses a one hidden layer MLP with 8192 hidden units (instead of 8192) and β=0.01𝛽0.01\beta=0.01. 8 “𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-DIB” uses the correct one hidden layer MLP with 128 hidden units and β=10𝛽10\beta=10.

D.2 CIFAR10+MNIST Dataset

We follow Achille and Soatto [20] and overlay MNIST digits on top of CIFAR10 images to create the CIFAR10+MNIST dataset. Concretely, we pick a CIFAR10 image and on top of it overlay an MNIST image selected uniformly at random. The code used to generate the dataset as well as some samples can be found in https://github.com/YannDubs/Overlayed-Datasets.

D.3 Correlation

For the correlation experiments in Sec. 4.3, we largely follow previous work by Jiang et al. [50] in the sweeps over hyperparameters to get an initial set of models with potentially different generalization errors.

Let Conv(kernel_size, stride) denote a convolutional layer. The basic block of the convolutional networks consist of (in order): Conv(3, 2, padding=1), BatchNorm, Relu, Conv(1, 1), BatchNorm, Relu, Conv(1,1), Relu, dropout. The final networks consist of one Conv(1,1),Relu used to set the correct number of channels, followed by “depth” number of blocks, followed by Conv(1,1) that set the number of channels to the dimensionality of the representation, followed by an average pooling over the spatial dimensions. The resulting output is a (deterministic) representation which will go through an MLP with 2 hidden layers of width 128 to perform classification.

In order to be comparable to Jiang et al. [50] we sweep over the following hyperparameters: 1 the learning rate (1e-3, 3e-4, 1e-4); 2 the batch size (32, 64, 128); 3 the dropout rate (0, 0.25, 0.5); 4 the width/channel size (192, 384, 768); 5 the depth/number of blocks (2, 4, 8); 6 the dimensionality of the representation (32, 128, 512). We train every models with combination of these parameters on CIFAR10 and stop once the train log likelihood is better than 0.01 (with a hard stop at 300 epochs if the model did not reach that threshold by then). The resulting subset of 562 models thus all (approximately) perform equally well on training, which enables to study the effect of hyperparameters on generalization in isolation without the influence of performance on training as an indicator for generalization. For each resulting model we compute the difference between performance on train and test (generalization gap), both in terms of accuracy and log likelihood. We then compare the rank correlation between the desired measure and the observed generalization gap.

The methods that we compare to are the best performing in each section of Jiang et al. [50], namely: 1 “Entropy” is the average entropy of the predicted probabilities; 2 “Path Norm” takes an input of all ones and passes it through the network where all the parameters are squared and returns the square root of the sumed logits; 3 “Var. Grad.” computes the average gradients at the end of training; 4 “Sharp. Mag” essentially finds the maximum (relative) perturbation that can be applied to the weights to get less than 0.1 log likelihood difference. We use 1α′1superscript𝛼′\frac{1}{\alpha^{\prime}} version of sharpness magnitude as described in Jiang et al. [50].

The code of Jiang et al. [50] is not (currently) public but we did our best to follow their work on all but the following three points: 1 We use an MLP after the CNN, which was used to evaluate 𝒱+superscript𝒱\mathcal{V}^{+},𝒱−superscript𝒱\mathcal{V}^{-} minimality as in the rest of the paper, 2 We do not sweep over the weight decay and optimizer but instead we vary the size of the representation, to try to incorporate a representation-specific parameter, 3 our implementation of the sharpness magnitude measures differences in log-likelihood instead of accuracy. 151515We initially only wanted to consider generalization in terms of log-likelihood since our theory only talks about log-likelihood. For this reason, the correlation of sharpness magnitude in table 2 is lower than in Jiang Jiang et al. [50], which is why we also transcribe their results.

Appendix E Additional Experiments

In the rest of the appendices we provide additional experiments and results. Specifically we investigate: 1 How to obtain meaningful nested predictive families 𝒱−⊂𝒱⊂𝒱+superscript𝒱𝒱superscript𝒱\mathcal{V}^{-}\subset\mathcal{V}\subset\mathcal{V}^{+} which we use throughout our paper (Sec. E.1); 2 Different methods to deal with the min-max optimization in ℒDIBsubscriptℒDIB\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DIB}}{} (Sec. E.2); 3 An important “trick” that helps the min-max optimization of ℒDIBsubscriptℒDIB\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DIB}}{} (Sec. E.3); 4 The effect of using Monte Carlo estimation of I𝒱⁡[Z→Dec​(X,𝒴)]subscriptI𝒱→ZDecX𝒴\operatorname{I_{\mathcal{V}}}\negthinspace\left[\mathrm{Z}\rightarrow\mathrm{Dec}(\mathrm{X},\mathcal{Y}){}\right]{} (Sec. E.4); 5 How to improve ℒDIBsubscriptℒDIB\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DIB}}{} by sampling approximately independent nuisance r.v.s from Dec​(X,y)DecX𝑦\mathrm{Dec}(\mathrm{X},y){} (Sec. E.5); 6 How to efficiently implement ℒDIBsubscriptℒDIB\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DIB}}{} for standard GPU batch training (Sec. E.6); 7 How to obtain an ERM which performs well on train but bad on test (“Worst ERM”;Sec. E.7); 8 Whether our 𝒱−s​u​f​f​i​c​i​e​n​c​y𝒱𝑠𝑢𝑓𝑓𝑖𝑐𝑖𝑒𝑛𝑐𝑦\mathcal{V}-sufficiency results in Sec. 4.1 hold across various settings (Sec. E.8); 9 Why 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-sufficiency is not as important in large networks trained with SGD (Sec. E.9); 10 The effect of β𝛽\beta on different 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality terms (Sec. E.10); 11 The performance of DIB as a standard regularizer (Sec. E.11); 12 Whether the degree of 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}-minimality is correlated with generalization across different neural networks and datasets (Sec. E.12).

E.1 Sweeping over Predictive Families

A core set of our experiments involve using nested predictive families 𝒱−⊂𝒱⊂𝒱+superscript𝒱𝒱superscript𝒱\mathcal{V}^{-}\subset\mathcal{V}\subset\mathcal{V}^{+}. In this appendix, we study different ways of “sweeping” over functional families, i.e. finding some parameter s.t. increasing the value it can take k<k′𝑘superscript𝑘′k<k^{\prime} means increasing the family 𝒱k⊂𝒱k′subscript𝒱𝑘subscript𝒱superscript𝑘′\mathcal{V}_{k}\subset\mathcal{V}_{k^{\prime}}. Using neural networks with varying architectures, we investigate the following possibilities:

Width

Sweeping over the width (w=4k𝑤superscript4𝑘w=4^{k}) of a single layer MLP (d=1𝑑1d=1).

Depth

Sweeping over the depth (d=k𝑑𝑘d=k) of an MLP (w=128𝑤128w=128) 161616We also tried with a width of 32 but the differences due to depth was surprisingly less pronounced there..

Width and Depth

Simultaneously sweeping over the depth (d=k𝑑𝑘d=k) and width (w=32∗2k𝑤32superscript2𝑘w=32*2^{k}) of an MLP.

Weight Pruning

Sweeping over the percentage of non-pruned weights (%≠0=2k28\%_{\neq 0}=\frac{2^{k}}{2^{8}}) of an MLP (d=3𝑑3d=3,w=2048𝑤2048w=2048). 171717To implement that, we start with a usual MLP and then prune recursively 50% of the weights. The recursiveness ensures that every weight which were previously pruned will also be pruned in the next round.

To see whether the aforementioned methods are effective ways of sweeping over functional families, we analyze their respective complexity by looking at how well they can fit arbitrary labelling, which was proposed by [37] as a measure of complexity intuitively similar to Rademacher complexity. Specifically, we train a 𝒳−1024−1024−𝒵−64−𝒴𝒳10241024𝒵64𝒴\mathcal{X}-1024-1024-\mathcal{Z}-64-\mathcal{Y} MLP on CIFAR10, then freeze the encoder 𝒳−1024−1024−𝒵𝒳10241024𝒵\mathcal{X}-1024-1024-\mathcal{Z}, shuffle the labels PZ×Y=PZ×PYsubscript𝑃ZYsubscript𝑃Zsubscript𝑃YP_{\mathrm{Z}\times\mathrm{Y}}=P_{\mathrm{Z}}\times P_{\mathrm{Y}}, and compute the training log likelihood achieved by the predictive family minf∈𝒱⁡R^​(f,Z;𝒟)subscript𝑓𝒱^R𝑓Z𝒟\min_{f\in\mathcal{V}}\hat{\mathrm{R}}(f,\mathrm{Z};\mathcal{D}). We do so for increasing dimensionality (2,16,1024) of the representations ZZ\mathrm{Z}.

Figure 6 shows that each of the four aforementioned sweeping methods increases their respective complexities (besides for two dimensional representations which appears constant). Sweeping only over depth does not appear to significantly increase the complexity of the functional family 181818This is likely because the sweeping interval [1,…,5]1…5[1,\dots,5] is quite small. When using a larger sweeping interval, the optimization was harder, often yielding smaller randomized log likelihood.. Sweeping over weight pruning fraction is a very effective method to increase the functional family. Sweeping over the width and depth together is also very effective to increase the complexity of the family, but we found that in some experiments the deepest MLPs were too difficult to optimize. Sweeping over the width of the MLP increases the complexity significantly. This last method is simple and effective, so we decided to use it as the sweeping method in the main text.

Exact

Assuming that we can perform the inner optimization exactly fY∗=arg⁡minf∈𝒱⁡R(Y)​(f,Z)subscriptsuperscript𝑓Ysubscript𝑓𝒱superscriptRY𝑓Zf^{*}_{\mathrm{Y}}=\arg\min_{f\in\mathcal{V}}\mathrm{R}^{(\mathrm{Y})}(f,\mathrm{Z}) and fN∗=arg⁡maxf∈𝒱⁡R(N)​(f,Z)subscriptsuperscript𝑓Nsubscript𝑓𝒱superscriptRN𝑓Zf^{*}_{\mathrm{N}}=\arg\max_{f\in\mathcal{V}}\mathrm{R}^{(\mathrm{N})}(f,\mathrm{Z}), then we we know by the Envelop theorem [101] that the gradients are simply:

∂∂Z​R(Y)​(fY∗,Z)+β′​∑y∈𝒴∑N∈Dec​(X,y)∂∂Z​R(Y)​(fN∗,Z)ZsuperscriptRYsubscriptsuperscript𝑓YZsuperscript𝛽′subscript𝑦𝒴subscriptNDecX𝑦ZsuperscriptRYsubscriptsuperscript𝑓NZ\frac{\partial}{\partial\mathrm{Z}}\mathrm{R}^{(\mathrm{Y})}(f^{*}_{\mathrm{Y}},\mathrm{Z})+\beta^{\prime}\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\sum_{\mathrm{N}\in\mathrm{Dec}(\mathrm{X},y){}}\frac{\partial}{\partial\mathrm{Z}}\mathrm{R}^{(\mathrm{Y})}(f^{*}_{\mathrm{N}},\mathrm{Z})

This exact method is very restrictive, as we can essentially only find the optimal functions if we add strong restrictions on 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V} (e.g. linear classifiers).

Joint Optimization

One could disregard the issues that arise from min-max optimization and optimize everything jointly. This can easily be implemented by reversing the sign (sometimes referred to as a gradient reversal layer [102]). This is what we show in fig. 2(b). Note that there are no guarantees of convergence, even to a local minimum.

Unrolling Optimization

A third possibility consists in “unrolling” the inner optimization [103, 104, 39, 105] by taking a few SGD steps in the internal optimization loop (over the functions f𝑓f) and computing the gradients with respect to the ZZ\mathrm{Z}. Note that there are again no guarantees of converging even to a local minimum. Nevertheless, the gradients are better estimates of the true gradients than in the joint case. A key hyper-parameter then becomes the number of inner optimization steps to perform for each Z𝑍Z update.

We experimented with the three aforementioned approaches to estimating the gradients. While preliminary results suggested that the “Exact” method is, unsurprisingly, better than the two other methods, we did not want to restrict the function families and thus opted for the other two approaches. In the following, we compare two performance of the other methods that do not necessitate any restriction on 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}. For all of experiments, we employ an additional trick that arises due to the inner optimization not being run until convergence (see Sec. E.3).

Figure 7 shows the effect of the number of inner optimization steps on Alice’s generalization. We see that she achieves best performance by either joint optimization (which is noted as 0 inner optimization steps) or unrolling optimization with multiple inner optimization steps. Although it is not clear from fig. 7 using 555 inner optimization steps is significantly better than performing joint optimization. Indeed, at the best β𝛽\beta (β=10𝛽10\beta=10 for 5 inner steps, and β=1000𝛽1000\beta=1000 for joint optimization) taking 5 inner steps gives an average test log likelihood of −1.56±0.03plus-or-minus1.560.03-1.56\pm 0.03 against −1.65±0.00plus-or-minus1.650.00-1.65\pm 0.00 for joint optimization. We also see that increasing the number of steps results in an objective which appears more robust to the choice of β𝛽\beta. This comes, however, at the cost of increased computational complexity. Throughout the paper we use five inner optimization steps, but note that for larger problems, it would be advisable to use joint optimization in order to decrease the computational complexity.

E.3 Diverging Representation from Min-Max

As discussed in Sec. E.2, the DIB objective requires a minimax optimization, which we solve using 5 steps of inner optimization. A major issue that arises from with this approach is that the encoder can “cheat” because the inner optimization is not done until convergence. As a result the encoder can learn representations ZZ\mathrm{Z} that are highly variable such that the decoder f∈𝒱𝑓𝒱f\in\mathcal{V}, which tries to predict NN\mathrm{N}, cannot adapt quickly enough.

To solve this issue we pass the sampled representations through a batch normalization layer [106] but without trainable hyper-parameters, i.e. we normalize each batch of representations to have a mean of zero and a variance of one. As this is simply a rescaling, it could easily be learned by any f∈𝒱𝑓𝒱f\in\mathcal{V} if the inner optimization were performed until convergence (it does not modify 𝒱𝒱\mathcal{V}). Nevertheless, it does give much better results since it ensures that the encoder learns a meaningful representation, rather than taking advantage of the limited number of steps in the internal maximization. Note that the encoder has many more parameters than the classifier, allowing it to alter the representation such that the classifier cannot “keep up”. Figure 8 shows that without this “trick” the mean and standard deviation in fact diverges as β𝛽\beta increases (labeled DIB Free). This is solved by the normalization trick (labeled DIB), which we use throughout the paper.
